New Mexico forensic laboratory emphasizes scientific integrity and advanced technology
The New Mexico Department of Public Safety Forensic Laboratory underscores its commitment to accuracy through advanced technology and extensive staff training. Serving hundreds of agencies statewide from three regional facilities—including a newly expanded lab—the team stresses objective science over dramatized portrayals.
The New Mexico Department of Public Safety Forensic Laboratory is highlighted as a center for scientific precision and integrity, where expert analysts, rigorous training, and modern technology work together to support justice, according to an Oct. 15 announcement.
The laboratory conducts a wide range of forensic examinations including firearms and toolmark analysis, DNA testing, latent fingerprint identification, controlled substances analysis, fire debris investigation, and evidence processing. The mission is to provide unbiased results that serve the people of New Mexico. Dr. William Watson, Quality Assurance Director for the Forensic Laboratory, said, “We play a support role for law enforcement, but we are not law enforcement. We play a support role for the judicial system, but again, we’re not the legal system. We’re scientists who act as advocates for the evidence.”
Staffed by 52 employees—including DNA analysts, chemists, latent print examiners, firearms experts and administrative personnel—the laboratory requires most scientific positions to have at least a bachelor’s degree in relevant fields. It operates three regional labs in Santa Fe, Las Cruces and Hobbs that serve approximately 300 law enforcement agencies as well as state and federal courts throughout New Mexico.
In Fiscal Year 2026 alone, forensic scientists analyzed more than 18,918 evidence items from 6,715 criminal cases statewide and appeared in court on 577 occasions related to trials or hearings. Employees undergo intensive training lasting up to four years depending on discipline; this includes internal programs supplemented by nationally recognized instruction along with competency assessments after initial training and annual proficiency tests.
Watson said advances in forensic technology have improved capabilities significantly: “Our laboratory is equipped with state-of-the-art forensic technology... Each piece of equipment has a different purpose in essentially meeting the mission.” The new Santa Fe facility opened in 2024 is four times larger than its predecessor—allowing greater collaboration among disciplines—and features specialized spaces such as an on-site firearms testing range.
Dispelling common misconceptions about their work environment or roles popularized by television dramas or movies—such as secretive labs or badge-wielding scientists—Watson said, “One of the things pop culture often gets wrong is the idea that we do a lot of experimentation... That’s not the way it works. We work with very specific protocols and procedures that have been validated... Mad scientists don’t exist in our field.” He concluded by emphasizing staff dedication: “Everyone here works very hard to do the best job they can... We are advocates for the evidence... we are not for one side or the other.”
